question.text: What is the concept of "segregated portfolio" (side-pocketing) introduced by SEBI for mutual fund debt schemes?

answer.text: Separating distressed/downgraded securities into a separate portfolio to protect existing investors from forced redemption losses
Creating a separate portfolio exclusively for high-net-worth investors within the same scheme
Maintaining a separate portfolio of liquid assets to meet redemption demands
Dividing the scheme portfolio into equity and debt segments for balanced funds

explanation.text: The Logic: Per NISM Series V-A workbook, a segregated portfolio separates debt or money-market instruments affected by a credit event from the main portfolio (p79, p260-p261). Page 79 defines side-pocketing as separating distressed/illiquid assets from the more liquid assets of the scheme. On creation, existing unitholders receive an equal number of units in the segregated portfolio (p261), and the segregated units are listed within 10 working days. The Trap: Option C describes a liquidity buffer, not side-pocketing. Option B's investor-type segregation is prohibited under the fair-treatment principle (p253-p254, p259). Option D describes asset allocation in balanced funds, not the credit-event mechanism in side-pocketing. Note: No subscription or redemption is allowed in the segregated portfolio. Recoveries from the distressed assets, when realized, are distributed to investors who held units in the segregated portfolio on the date of its creation (p259-p262).
